To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the neural signal underlying CN is a linear combination of three components with different time constants and that the unstable component is tentatively identified with the eye position feedback signal.
congenital nystagnus has a neural signal that is approximately linear and has three degrees of freedom and the three time constants of the neural signal are 7–9 ms, 22–70 ms and 31–32 ms.
congenital nystamgus is an oscillation that is generated by a neural signal with 3 degrees-of-freedom.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the neural mechanisms that underlie congenital nystamgus and the normal eye movement control system.
a quantitative description of the neural signal that underlies congenital nystamgus.

the development and application of a new technique for time series analysis of eye movement data, and with the application of this new technique to the analysis of the abnormal eye movements of patients with congenital nysta-gmus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the neural signal underlying the congenital nystatagmus waveform is generated by an approximately linear system with 3 degrees freedom and that the unstable component is most likely the eye position signal in the superior collicular oculomotor pathway.
the neural signal underlying the congenital nystatagmus oscillation is a combination of normal saccade and slide signals with an unstable component that is probably the eye position signal.

the neural signal underlying the oscillation of congenital nystags is generated by a system with three degrees of freedom, which has a stable component that resembles the normal oculometric signal, and an unstable component that is not well understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neural signal underlying nystagmus has a structure similar to that of the normal saccadic and smooth pursuit system.

, although the normal eye movement signal and the neural signal underlying the congenital nystatgum are both composed of a saccade signal, a slide signal and an eye position signal, the latter is unstable and the former is stable.
congenital nystgamous waveforms are generated by an unstable system with a linear model in which a saccadic burst, slide and unstable signal are combined.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the neural signal underlying nystagmus may have components that are similar to the normal oculor motor system.
the time constants of the neural signal in congenital nystatgus can be used to infer the underlying neural mechanisms.
the neural signal underlying the congenital nystagnus waveform can be characterised by the same components as the normal oculmotor system.
